The one-tap 'snooze/remind tomorrow' right in the push is the key detail — it makes a wrong guess cost nothing, which is what makes adaptive reminders feel helpful rather than presumptuous. Minor risk: needs a sensible cold-start default before two weeks of data exist.
feasibilityNote: No legal risk. Needs a real backend (GitHub Pages alone can't send timed push): Web Push + service worker with VAPID, a per-user 'usual time' calc job, and notification action buttons (snooze/tomorrow) wired to service-worker click handlers that reschedule server-side. All doable on a free-tier serverless function + cron (Supabase/Firebase/Cloudflare Workers), but it's the app's first real infra piece, not a static-site feature.

title: Split-session logging across books
description: Mid-session, a 'Switch book' control lets a reader log time against a second book in the same sitting (e.g., 20 minutes of an audiobook during a commute, then 15 minutes of an ebook before bed) without ending and restarting the timer twice — each portion is attributed to its own book's totals automatically.
usabilityNote: Useful for a real behavior, but mid-session book-switching adds a decision point and mental bookkeeping (which minutes went to which book) that risks confusing users about what's currently being tracked, especially in a quick web session.
desirabilityNote: Real use case (commute audiobook + bedtime ebook) but adds a mid-flow decision point to what should be the app's simplest interaction. Power users will love it; casual readers may never notice it exists or find switching mid-timer fiddly.
feasibilityNote: Requires tracking two concurrent time allocations and splitting elapsed time between two book records — more branching state than a single timer, but still pure app logic, no backend complexity.

title: Smart Shelves
description: Users create rule-based shelves that auto-populate and stay live, e.g. 'Unread & under 300 pages,' 'By authors I've read before,' or 'Sitting untouched 6+ months.' A simple builder lets you chain 2-3 conditions with dropdowns (no query language), and books animate in/out of the shelf as their status changes elsewhere in the app.
usabilityNote: Auto-updating shelves are appealing, but any rule builder — even dropdown-only with 2-3 conditions — asks casual readers to think in boolean logic, which is a step up in cognitive load from tapping a tag or button. Great for power users, friction-prone for the average reader.
desirabilityNote: This pattern (smart playlists, live photo albums) is proven to be beloved wherever it appears because it automates a chore readers actually do manually otherwise (re-sorting by page count, mood, author). A 2-3 condition dropdown builder keeps it from feeling like a database query tool, which is the right scope.
feasibilityNote: Needs a small condition-chaining rule engine and reactive recompute whenever any book's status/last-read-date changes (e.g. 'untouched 6+ months' requires tracking last-interaction timestamps). More edge cases than #1/#2 but still no external dependency or infra cost.

title: Physical Copy & Lending Tracker
description: For books marked 'physical,' an optional detail panel tracks shelf location (e.g. 'living room,' 'boxed - storage') and lending status ('lent to Maya, due back Oct 5'), with a small hand-off icon on the cover when a copy is out on loan. Addresses the real-world 'who has my book' problem no reading tracker currently solves.
usabilityNote: Genuinely useful, but it's a form-filling flow (typing a shelf location, a borrower's name, a due date) rather than a tap/gesture interaction, so it breaks the app's otherwise light, animated feel. Also easy to let go stale since nothing prompts the user to update 'due back' status.
desirabilityNote: Solves a real and relatable problem (forgetting who borrowed your book), but it's an opt-in data-entry feature that only pays off if you keep it updated — many users will set it up once, forget to log a loan, and lose trust in it. Enjoyable and useful for the subset who lend books often; low pull for e-reader-only or don't-lend readers.
feasibilityNote: Just extra optional text/date fields (location, borrower, due date) on the physical-copy record. No infra needed unless you add due-date reminders (still easy with client-side notifications or a simple scheduled email).

title: "Which Did You Like More?" Calibrator
description: After rating a book, users occasionally see a forced-choice screen with two covers from their own read history and "Which did you like more?" — one tap swipes the loser away. These picks quietly calibrate what a "4-star" means for that reader and build a drag-reorderable personal all-time-favorites ladder.
usabilityNote: The single swipe-away tap is easy, but the screen appears unprompted with no visible reason ('quietly calibrates'), which can feel random; users may not understand why they're being asked or what it's for.
desirabilityNote: The Elo-style forced-choice mechanic has proven appeal (see Beli), but surfacing it unprompted after every rating risks feeling like an interruption/chore rather than a reward unless frequency is tightly controlled.
feasibilityNote: Needs a small pairwise-comparison/Elo-style algorithm (a few dozen lines of math) and a drag-reorder list (dnd-kit/SortableJS handles that). Slightly more design work than the others to pick pairs sensibly and avoid feeling random/annoying, but still no backend beyond storing comparison results. No legal risk.

title: Author hub flip-card
description: Tapping the author's name on a book detail page flips the hero card over (like a page turn) to reveal an author mini-profile: short bio, photo, and a horizontally scrolling strip of their other books' covers with an animated stagger-in. Tapping any cover in the strip flies the user into that book's own detail page, making author exploration a fluid side-trip rather than a full navigation away from the current book.
desirabilityNote: A fun, low-cost way to surface an author's backlist without a full navigation detour, and the flip animation fits the app's playful tone; scores below the top tier because author browsing is a secondary use case for most readers, not a core loop they'll use often.
feasibilityNote: CSS 3D flip is easy. Author bio/photo and 'other books by this author' data can come from Open Library's Author API (free, legitimate) or Wikidata, though bios/photos are inconsistently populated for lesser-known authors — a data-gap issue to handle gracefully (e.g. fallback placeholder), not a legal or infra one.

title: Indie bookstore finder for physical copies
description: For the physical-copy option, instead of defaulting straight to Amazon, the panel queries Bookshop.org to show the price and a 'supports an indie bookstore' label, with an optional 'pick your store' step that lets the purchase credit a specific local shop the reader chooses from a short list, animated as a map-pin drop when selected.
desirabilityNote: Values-driven readers will love supporting a local shop; price-first shoppers may see it as an extra step before reaching Amazon. Good as a visible option, riskier as a default.
feasibilityNote: Bookshop.org runs an actual public affiliate program/API designed for exactly this use case, including routing sales to a specific local store — well-trodden, documented, and legal (this is how most indie reading apps already do it). Main friction is affiliate account approval, which is a form to fill out, not an engineering problem.

title: Chapter-Gated Club Rooms
description: Create or join a small club around one book; the discussion thread is split into chapter-by-chapter 'rooms' that stay locked (shown greyed with a padlock) until you've logged reaching that chapter, and a club admin can pin one discussion question per room -- Fable's chapter-room mechanic without needing celebrity branding to feel worth joining.
usabilityNote: Splitting discussion into multiple locked/unlocked rooms adds navigation overhead compared to a single thread, and users must keep their logged progress in sync with room boundaries or find themselves confused about which room is currently open. The padlock visual helps, but the overall structure is more to learn and manage than a flat club discussion.
desirabilityNote: This is Fable's proven, well-loved mechanic for exactly the reason stated: group discussion is where spoiler anxiety is worst. Removing the celebrity-book-club gating and letting any small group get this is a clear upgrade, not a gimmick -- readers who do book clubs will actively want this.
feasibilityNote: Club membership + threaded discussion + a per-user 'unlocked' check against their own progress is more moving parts (club CRUD, thread CRUD, admin-pin field) than a typical social feature, but nothing exotic — just more surface area to build/test solo.

title: Two-person Book Buddy shared goal meter
description: A lightweight, positive-sum pairing feature: two friends (or a small book-club pair) link up around one shared book or a shared monthly minutes goal, and each person's reading fills the same joint progress bar shown on both profiles. Reaching 100% unlocks a joint 'Buddy Badge' animation for both users simultaneously. Deliberately excludes Habitica's damage/boss-battle punishment mechanic -- if one buddy lags, the bar just fills slower, nobody 'takes damage.'
usabilityNote: The shared bar itself is dead simple to read, but the feature depends on a second person actually engaging — pairing/invite flow, agreeing on a shared book or goal, and one partner's inactivity silently stalling the bar are all friction points and failure modes outside the user's own control.
desirabilityNote: Book-buddy/duo reading is a real, beloved social pattern, and the positive-sum design (bar fills slower, nobody 'takes damage') smartly avoids Habitica's punishment backlash. Ceiling is that it requires finding a willing partner, so it's a great feature for the reader who has one and irrelevant to the many who don't.
feasibilityNote: Needs a lightweight pairing/invite flow and a progress value two accounts both read/write — straightforward on a small hosted backend (Supabase/Firebase realtime tier), but it is a second backend feature (beyond solo-user state) so it's more work than the single-user badge/streak ideas. No legal risk.

title: Visual Spine-View Shelf
description: A toggle switches the library from grid/list into a skeuomorphic bookshelf of vertical spines colored and sized from real cover art, grouped onto 'shelves' that fill and wrap like a physical bookcase. Dragging a spine to reorder it produces a satisfying nudge-and-settle animation among its neighbors, giving the library a tactile, personal feel other trackers' spreadsheet-like lists lack.
usabilityNote: Delightful and tactile, but skeuomorphic shelves have real usability costs at scale: spine text is hard to scan for dozens/hundreds of books, drag affordance may not be obvious, and wrapping shelf layout is tricky to get right responsively on small screens.
desirabilityNote: High emotional/aesthetic payoff — readers already photograph and admire physical shelves, so a tactile virtual equivalent taps into real behavior (see BookTok shelfie culture). Risk is it's a 'browse once, then switch back to grid' novelty since spines are worse than covers for actually finding a specific book, but as an optional toggle it's pure upside.
feasibilityNote: No infra/legal risk, but real engineering lift: extracting a spine color from cover art (canvas pixel sampling), a shelf-wrapping layout algorithm, and a convincing 'nudge-and-settle' physics-like animation is meaningfully harder than a standard list/grid. Budget real design+animation time; not a quick build.

title: Swipeable edition & cover carousel
description: A horizontally swipeable strip on the detail page lets users browse different covers, translations, anniversary editions, and reprints of the same book side by side, each card flipping slightly on swipe like a physical stack of covers. Purely a visual/identification aid (distinct from any buy-this-edition pricing flow) that helps readers confirm 'is this the edition I remember' or admire cover art.
desirabilityNote: Nice for cover-art enthusiasts and collectors trying to identify 'the edition I remember,' but it's a niche interest most casual readers won't use often; the swipe/flip animation is pleasant but the feature itself is closer to a delightful extra than something readers would ask for.
feasibilityNote: UI is a standard swipeable carousel (CSS scroll-snap or a small JS lib). Data dependency is the real factor: pulling multiple editions/covers per work from Open Library's Editions API or Google Books is free and legitimate, but coverage/quality of alternate covers varies and may need manual curation for popular titles.

title: Margin Notes (Spoiler-Locked)
description: Friends can leave a short note or emoji reaction anchored to a specific page/chapter of a book you're both reading; the note stays blurred with a lock icon on your copy until your own progress bar passes that page, then it unlocks with a gentle reveal animation -- Fable's in-text social annotation done spoiler-safe by construction.
usabilityNote: The reveal animation and blur-until-you-catch-up mechanic is intuitive in concept, but it depends on precise page/chapter position matching between the note-writer and reader's own edition or format, which is a common source of mismatched or prematurely-unlocked spoilers. Users may not understand why a note stays locked or unlocks 'early.'
desirabilityNote: Fable's in-text annotation is one of the most-praised social reading features that exists today, and solving it 'spoiler-safe by construction' rather than by trust/tagging is a genuine UX improvement. Only ding: leaving anchored notes is manual effort, so it'll be used by a passionate minority rather than everyone.
feasibilityNote: The blocking issue isn't legal, it's data: 'page/chapter' isn't a stable unit across editions/ebook/audiobook formats, so anchoring a note to 'page 214' and gating it on 'your progress' requires a normalized progress metric (e.g. % complete) per book, which is nontrivial to build well. Doable but the hardest idea in this list to get right.

title: Opt-in weekly Reading Leagues
description: Bronze-through-Diamond league brackets (Duolingo-style) that only activate if a user explicitly opts in and invites friends or a book club -- default is off, and there's a one-tap 'leave league' with no penalty. Ranking is by minutes-read or pages, resets every Monday so a bad week never permanently locks anyone out, and promotion/demotion zones are shown as a simple animated ladder. Solves Strava's 'comparison anxiety/humblebragging' complaint by keeping it private-by-default and per-friend-group rather than global.
usabilityNote: Default-off and one-tap exit keep it frictionless for anyone who ignores it, but for participants there are several concepts to learn at once (bracket tier, promotion/demotion zone, weekly reset, invite flow), and inviting a friend/book club is a real setup step, not a single tap.
desirabilityNote: Well-designed against Strava's comparison-anxiety backlash (opt-in, private, no-penalty exit, weekly reset), but reading is inherently more solitary than fitness — most users won't have a friend group to league with, so this likely delights a vocal minority (book clubs) rather than the general reader.
feasibilityNote: The one idea here that outgrows static GitHub Pages hosting: needs real user accounts, friend/group invites, a weekly reset job, and league-bracket state shared across users — doable on a free-tier backend (Supabase/Firebase) but it's a genuine backend, not a page feature. No legal risk since it's private-by-default and opt-in, but meaningfully more build/maintenance surface than the rest of the list.

title: Per-day reminder schedule
description: Reminder settings let a user set a different time (or 'off') for each day of the week via a 7-segment toggle row — e.g. 8pm on weeknights, no reminder Saturday, noon Sunday — fixing Serial Reader's most-cited complaint about a single rigid daily delivery time. Changes take effect immediately with a small checkmark animation confirming the new cadence.
usabilityNote: The 7-segment toggle row is a compact, visual way to set a weekly schedule (similar to alarm apps), and the instant checkmark confirmation is good feedback. Still inherently more decisions than a single time picker, so it's a step up in power at a real, if small, cost in setup friction for casual users.
desirabilityNote: Genuinely fixes a documented complaint (rigid single daily time), but it's a settings-screen power-feature that most casual users will set once and forget, or never touch. Useful and not at all gimmicky, just modest in day-to-day delight — a quality-of-life fix rather than something readers will rave about.
feasibilityNote: UI (7-toggle grid) is trivial; the hard part is firing a push at N different times/day per user across timezones, which requires a scheduled server job (not static hosting) — same backend as idea #1/#9, just with more schedule slots to check. No legal concern, just a moderate always-on infra dependency instead of a one-off script.

title: Crowd tag-mirror cloud on detail page
description: The book detail page shows a tag cloud of how OTHER readers have tagged the book (mood, tone, content warnings, tropes), with tag size scaled to how often readers used it — a modernized, animated take on LibraryThing's Tag Mirror. Tapping a tag filters the reviews section below to reviews mentioning that theme. Kept visually distinct from the user's own personal shelving tags.
desirabilityNote: Useful signal for discovery, but tag clouds are a dated, low-information-density UI pattern that readers mostly skim past rather than engage with; separating it from personal shelving tags avoids confusion but doesn't add excitement on its own.
feasibilityNote: Tag storage + frequency-sized cloud is trivial DB/UI work. Feasible IF 'filters reviews mentioning that theme' means reviews the reviewer themselves tagged with that word (structured match, easy). If it instead means text-mining review prose for thematic mentions, that's NLP work and the score drops to ~4. Build the structured version.

title: Trust-weighted review sort & filter bar
description: Above the reviews list on the detail page, a pill toolbar lets users sort by Most Helpful / Highest / Lowest / Most Recent and filter by star count, with the default sort weighting reviews from readers whose past ratings correlate with the current user's taste ahead of raw chronological order. This directly counters Goodreads' review-bombing/sock-puppet problem by structurally de-emphasizing coordinated low-effort reviews rather than moderating them after the fact.
desirabilityNote: Directly attacks a well-known, widely complained-about pain point (Goodreads review-bombing/brigading) with a structural fix rather than moderation; readers who've been burned by unreliable review sorting would value this highly, though the taste-correlation weighting needs to feel transparent or it risks seeming manipulative.
feasibilityNote: The sort/filter pills themselves are trivial. The 'taste-correlation' default ranking is a mini recommender system (needs per-user rating vectors and a similarity computation, e.g. cosine/Pearson between the viewer and each reviewer) — buildable at small scale with a scheduled batch job, but it's real algorithm work and is useless/inaccurate until the app has enough users rating overlapping books (cold-start). Ship chronological + basic-helpful sort first; treat correlation ranking as a stretch goal.

title: Nameplate Finale
description: Onboarding ends with a short sequence of a quill animating the user's name in cursive onto a leather-look library card, which then becomes their permanent profile bookplate — a bespoke, ceremonial close to first-run setup instead of just dropping onto the home screen.
usabilityNote: Purely decorative capstone that adds a mandatory wait before reaching the app, and cursive rendering of arbitrary typed names is a legibility/i18n risk with no functional payoff.
desirabilityNote: Charming and on-theme for book lovers, but a one-time ceremonial animation the user cannot skip could feel indulgent or slow to anyone who just wants to start using the app; fine if it's short and skippable, less fine otherwise.
feasibilityNote: Animating arbitrary user-entered names in convincing cursive handwriting (SVG stroke-dasharray 'handwriting' effect) is the hard part -- it works great for fixed strings but arbitrary names/lengths need a cursive webfont traced as an SVG path, which is finicky to get looking hand-written rather than just a wipe-reveal. Doable solo but expect several iterations to avoid looking cheap. No legal risk, no infra.

title: Ink-Reveal Loading
description: Loading states (covers fetching, search results resolving) render as blank cream-colored pages where handwriting-style ink strokes animate in line by line, replacing generic gray shimmer skeletons with an on-brand placeholder that still clearly reads as 'loading.'
usabilityNote: Charming but loses skeleton screens' key job of previewing content shape, and a strokes-finish-but-content-still-missing state can read as frozen rather than clearly 'still loading.'
desirabilityNote: Loading states happen constantly and need to communicate 'wait' as fast and unambiguously as possible; a decorative handwriting animation is slower to parse than a shimmer skeleton and risks making waits feel longer, which is the opposite of what a loading state should do.
feasibilityNote: A reusable SVG stroke-animation placeholder is a solid, buildable skeleton-screen replacement with no backend dependency. Slightly more work than a generic shimmer since the 'ink line' shapes need designing, but it's a one-time component built once and reused everywhere. No legal/infra concerns.

title: Bundled, quiet-hours-aware notifications
description: Wink automatically defers any nudge that would land during the device's OS-level Do Not Disturb / quiet hours, and if more than one notification (reminder + weekly recap + 'almost finished') would fire the same day, it merges them into a single digest push instead of stacking pings — a direct fix for the notification-overload complaints leveled at Fable and BookBub.
usabilityNote: Entirely invisible, backend behavior — nothing for the user to configure or even notice except fewer, better-timed pings, which is about as frictionless as a feature can be. Slight risk is transparency: if a user doesn't get an expected nudge because of DND/merging logic they don't know exists, it can read as the app 'just not working' rather than as a feature.
desirabilityNote: This is closer to 'don't be annoying' hygiene than a delight feature, but that hygiene is exactly what users cite as their top complaint about competitor apps' notifications. High desirability as an invisible trust-builder, though it won't generate excitement on its own — it just prevents the single biggest reason people mute or uninstall a habit app.
feasibilityNote: Digest-merging same-day notifications into one push is easy server-side logic. But detecting OS-level Do Not Disturb / quiet hours from a website is not something the Web Push/Notification API exposes at all — that's a native-app-only capability. As written this is only partially buildable on web; would need to fall back to an in-app 'quiet hours' setting the user sets manually rather than reading real OS DND state. No legal risk, just a platform limitation.

title: "Still Feel the Same?" Check-In
description: Weeks after rating a book, once a few more titles in the same genre have been logged, the app occasionally surfaces a one-tap prompt on the library: "Still 4 stars for [Book]?" with a thumbs confirm or a quick re-slide-to-adjust control, letting ratings reflect how a book held up rather than a one-time first impression.
usabilityNote: The confirm/adjust interaction itself is trivial (one tap or a quick slide), but as an app-initiated interruption with unclear triggering logic it risks feeling like an unexplained nag rather than a user-initiated action.
desirabilityNote: Unprompted 'still 4 stars?' nags risk feeling intrusive and paternalistic rather than helpful; most readers don't want the app second-guessing a rating they already moved on from.
feasibilityNote: Doable with zero extra infra if triggered client-side on app open (check 'weeks since rating' + 'N more books logged in genre' against locally/DB-stored data) rather than via push notifications — that keeps it static-hosting-friendly. The real cost is product logic: tuning thresholds so it feels helpful rather than nagging takes iteration, and it's the one idea here where getting UX wrong could actively hurt retention. No legal risk.

title: 'Readers often mention' highlight chips
description: At the top of the reviews section, an auto-generated row of short phrase chips (e.g. 'slow start', 'twist ending', 'strong female lead') summarizes recurring points across all reviews, each chip showing how many reviews mention it. Tapping a chip filters the review list below to just those reviews, giving a scannable 'crowd consensus' entry point instead of forcing a scroll through dozens of full reviews to find a pattern.
desirabilityNote: Mirrors Amazon's proven 'customers say' review-summary feature, which readers already find genuinely useful for quickly gauging consensus without reading dozens of reviews; tapping to filter reviews is a natural, low-effort follow-through.
feasibilityNote: This is text-mining/summarization across many reviews per book. A cheap n-gram/keyword-frequency approach is buildable but tends to produce noisy or generic chips; a good version (like Amazon's AI review highlights) wants an LLM summarization pass per book, which is recurring inference cost and needs re-running as new reviews arrive. Also weak in early days when most books have few reviews (cold-start).

title: TBR-only deal feed
description: A dedicated in-app 'Deals' tab (no email) shows price-drop and free alerts filtered to only the books already sitting on the user's own want-to-read shelf, each card animating in with a strikethrough-old-price-to-new-price transition. No genre-wide blast, no daily newsletter, no stale 'still $9.99' noise -- just the handful of books the reader actually wants, the moment one of them gets cheap or free.
desirabilityNote: Solves the exact complaint people have about BookBub-style blasts: only notify me about books I actually want. High signal, zero noise, easy to love.
feasibilityNote: Filtering-to-shelf logic is trivial once you have a data source, but there's no public API for price-drop/free alerts (BookBub, Early Bird Books, Fussy Librarian are closed platforms) and Amazon's affiliate API has the same eligibility and caching restrictions as above. Doable via scraping Amazon's own Kindle deal listings, but that's a ToS gray area and a maintenance burden, not a clean build.

title: One-tap free sample reader
description: A 'Try a sample' button on the book detail page pulls the free preview/first-chapter excerpt from whichever retailer offers one (Kindle, Apple Books, Google Play, or a library 'read now' snippet) and opens it in a lightweight in-app reader overlay that slides up from the bottom, so a reader can sample a book before committing to a purchase or a weeks-long hold, without leaving Wink or juggling retailer apps.
desirabilityNote: Try-before-you-buy/borrow is a genuine decision aid, especially before committing to a weeks-long hold. In-app overlay keeps it frictionless rather than gimmicky.
feasibilityNote: Google Books API legitimately offers an embeddable preview widget and is free/well-documented, so this works for Google Play titles. Kindle and Apple Books have no public preview-embedding API, so 'whichever retailer offers one' really means 'Google Books only' in practice — solid MVP if scoped that way, overpromised as written.

title: Region-aware pricing
description: The app detects the user's country/currency and connected library systems automatically, so every price and every 'available' badge shown is one the user can actually act on -- no BookBub-style dead-end deals that turn out to be region-locked. A small 'showing offers for United States' chip is tappable to correct the detected region if it's wrong.
desirabilityNote: More of an expected baseline than a delight-inducing feature -- readers won't rave about it, but its absence (dead-end region-locked deals) is actively infuriating, so it's still strongly wanted.
feasibilityNote: Detecting country/currency via browser locale or IP geolocation is genuinely a one-line/native-API task with zero legal risk. The score is capped because the feature's value is entirely contingent on the same fragile pricing/library data from items 1 and 2 — the detection itself is easy, but 'actionable' prices behind it mostly aren't.

title: Natural-language mood search
description: The search bar accepts free text like 'cozy slow-burn fantasy under 400 pages' or 'dark reflective book like the one I just finished' and live-parses it into removable filter chips (mood, pace, length, genre) that animate in below the search box as they're recognized, letting the user fine-tune or delete a chip without retyping the whole query. Extends StoryGraph's mood/pacing metadata into the search bar itself instead of only post-hoc stats.
desirabilityNote: Directly answers a real, frequently-voiced reader want (StoryGraph's mood/pace filters are one of its most-loved features) and the removable-chip parsing makes the 'black box NLP' failure mode recoverable. Score held back one point because misparses of casual phrasing would feel frustrating rather than magical if the NLP isn't very good.
feasibilityNote: Two hard problems stacked: (1) parsing free text into mood/pace/length/genre reliably needs either an LLM call per keystroke-driven query (real, recurring AI-compute cost for a 'no big budget' project) or a brittle rule-based keyword parser with poor recall; (2) StoryGraph-style mood/pacing metadata doesn't exist for most books and would have to be crowdsourced or LLM-generated per title, which is itself a large ongoing cost/labor sink. Doable as a toy demo, not as the described experience.

title: Unified Get-This-Book panel
description: On every book's detail page, one expandable panel lists every acquisition path at once in a sortable table: ebook price on Kindle/Apple Books/Kobo, audiobook price on Audible/Libro.fm/Chirp, physical price on Bookshop.org/local indie/Amazon, and library ebook/audio availability via Libby/OverDrive/Hoopla with current wait time -- plus a public-domain link when one exists. A single sort toggle (Cheapest / Fastest / Free first) re-ranks the whole list instantly with a smooth row-reorder animation, so a reader never has to check five apps to know how to get a book.
desirabilityNote: Directly kills the real pain of checking five apps to find a book. Sortable price/wait/free comparison in one place is an obvious daily-use win, not a gimmick.
feasibilityNote: No public, free API exists for Kindle/Kobo pricing or Audible/Libro.fm/Chirp pricing; Amazon's Product Advertising API requires an active affiliate sales history (chicken-and-egg for a new app) and forbids caching prices >24h. Library availability via Libby/OverDrive is a closed, partnership-only API. Realistically this collapses to scraping 6+ sites, which is fragile and ToS-risky at solo-dev scale — the 'live sortable table across everything' promise isn't buildable safely today.

title: Buy-now-vs-wait threshold
description: When placing a library hold, a small inline slider lets the user set a personal patience threshold (e.g. 'if wait is over 3 weeks, show me a buy option instead'). If a hold's estimated wait exceeds it, the panel swaps the 'Place hold' button for a 'Skip the wait -- buy for $X' comparison card with a gentle cross-fade, directly answering Libby's most-cited complaint without forcing anyone to give up library-first by default.
desirabilityNote: Turns a common moment of hold-list frustration into a proactive, personalized option without abandoning library-first defaults. Feels smart rather than pushy.
feasibilityNote: Depends on both hold-wait data (item 2, not publicly available) and purchase pricing (item 1, largely not publicly available) — it inherits both underlying data gaps rather than adding new complexity of its own. The slider/UI logic is trivial; the blocker is having real numbers to feed it.

title: Taste Galaxy Map
description: An interactive, zoomable node-graph view where clusters of dots represent the user's genres/moods/authors, sized by how much they've enjoyed them, connected by soft glowing lines. Tapping a cluster gently pulls nearby unread book nodes into focus with a spring animation as fresh recommendations. Makes an abstract recommendation engine visible and explorable, rather than a flat list.
usabilityNote: Node-graph/zoomable-canvas navigation is a known usability trap for mainstream users -- it demands spatial exploration and trial-and-error panning/zooming, translates poorly to small or narrow web viewports, and doesn't map to any existing mental model of 'browsing books.'
desirabilityNote: Visually striking once, but a zoomable node-graph is a poor everyday tool for 'what should I read next' — novelty likely fades fast and it risks feeling like a tech demo over a feature.
feasibilityNote: Buildable with an off-the-shelf force-directed graph lib (d3-force, react-force-graph) — no backend needed, pure client-side. Feasible but the highest-effort UI item here: getting spring physics, zoom/pan, and legibility smooth at book-catalog scale takes real polish time for a solo dev, and it risks being a flashy centerpiece that's harder to use than a list. No legal risk.

title: Multi-library hold aggregator
description: Users link more than one library card (home county, work county, a library-anywhere card) in Settings. On a book's acquisition panel, instead of one 'place hold' button, a small carousel shows each linked library's copy count and estimated wait side by side, with the shortest-wait option visually highlighted, so hold-hopping across systems -- currently manual bookkeeping in Libby -- becomes a single obvious tap.
desirabilityNote: Huge for the subset of readers who already juggle multiple library cards (a known Libby power-user workaround); less relevant to casual single-library users, but never annoying to have.
feasibilityNote: OverDrive/Libby has no public third-party developer API; per-library wait-time and copy-count data is inaccessible without a formal OverDrive partnership. The only alternative is storing users' library card credentials and scraping their account pages, which is a security liability and a ToS violation, not a weekend feature.

title: Page-Turn Tab Transitions
description: Switching between the app's main sections (Library, Search, Profile) uses a paper page-turn/curl transition instead of a flat slide or fade, so the book metaphor shows up in ordinary navigation, not only when opening a book. CSS clip-path/transform keyframes kept under ~250ms so it never feels slow.
usabilityNote: Applying an ornate, linear 'page turn' to the highest-frequency action in the app (switching primary tabs) fights the tab-bar mental model of instant parallel views, and the cost compounds over hundreds of taps per session.
desirabilityNote: Applying a page-curl metaphor to routine, high-frequency navigation (every tab switch, many times a session) is a classic skeuomorphism trap -- it reads as cute for the first few switches and as friction thereafter, echoing the well-documented backlash against iOS page-curl UI.
feasibilityNote: A believable two-sided page-curl (not just a slide/fade) for arbitrary, variable-height real content is genuinely fiddly in CSS/clip-path and risks jank or looking flat if oversimplified; doing it on every single tab switch also raises perceived-speed risk if not kept fast. Recommend prototyping early since this is the riskiest 'core UX' animation to get feeling premium, but it's pure frontend -- no infra or legal issue.

title: One-tap calendar reading block
description: A settings toggle creates a recurring 'Reading time' event directly in the user's connected Google/Apple/Outlook calendar (via a downloadable .ics or OAuth calendar link) at their chosen time, so the reminder lives alongside real commitments instead of in a notification silo that's easy to dismiss. The event auto-updates if the user changes their reminder time in-app.
usabilityNote: The idea is simple, but the actual mechanics — OAuth consent screens for Google/Apple/Outlook, or downloading and manually opening an .ics file — are notoriously clunky on web and inconsistent across providers, undercutting the 'one-tap' framing. Auto-updating the event when the reminder time changes is a nice touch, but the initial connection step is real friction, not a false one.
desirabilityNote: Works well for a narrow slice of highly organized users who already calendar-block their life, but treating leisure reading like a scheduled meeting will feel heavy-handed or even off-putting to the average reader who wants reading to feel unscheduled and relaxing. Auto-writing into a personal/work calendar also raises a mild 'why is this app touching my calendar' friction point.
feasibilityNote: The .ics-download path is easy and needs zero infra (generate file client-side). The 'auto-updates via OAuth' path is a much bigger lift: Google Calendar OAuth consent screen + verification, token storage/refresh on a backend, and Outlook/Apple require separate integrations (Apple has no simple write API — CalDAV only). Ship the .ics version; treat live two-way sync as a stretch goal. No legal risk, just scope creep.

title: Live borrow-cap meter
description: For library services that cap monthly borrows (Hoopla-style), the acquisition panel shows a small live meter -- '4 of 8 borrows left this month, resets in 12 days' -- right next to the borrow button, updating in real time and pulsing amber near the limit, so a reader never taps 'borrow' only to discover the invisible system-wide cap has already kicked in.
desirabilityNote: Solves a real invisible-limit annoyance, but only matters to Hoopla-style borrowers, capping its broad appeal even though it's clearly useful for that group.
feasibilityNote: Hoopla's per-account borrow-cap and reset-date data is not exposed by any public API at all — it lives behind a logged-in library-patron session. Building this means storing and auto-logging-in with users' library credentials against an undocumented interface, which is both a security risk and almost certainly a ToS breach. Not buildable safely by a solo team.

title: Special-edition watch
description: A 'Watch for special editions' toggle on any book tracks signed copies, indie-press runs, illustrated/anniversary editions, and other collectible printings from retailers like Goldsboro, Illumicrate, or publisher direct stores; when one becomes available or restocks, a notification card slides in with a cover-flip animation showing the new edition's art, letting collectors catch limited runs they'd otherwise only find by chance.
desirabilityNote: Delightful for the collector niche (signed/illustrated editions), but most casual readers won't set this up or check it, making it more of a nice-to-have than a broadly desired feature.
feasibilityNote: Goldsboro, Illumicrate, and publisher-direct stores have no public inventory/restock APIs, so tracking them means scraping a growing set of small, frequently-changing sites — high ongoing maintenance for a solo dev and a ToS risk on each site. Feasible in spirit only if scoped down to 1-2 sources with RSS/stock-page polling, not the broad multi-retailer version described.
